title: Stripping the Common Factor Reduces to the Coprime Core
content: `general_homogeneous` handles `a·u + b·v = 0` for arbitrary `a = g·a'`, `b = g·b'`. The whole non-coprime case collapses to the coprime one in a single move: substituting the decomposition gives `g·(a'·u + b'·v) = 0`, and because `g ≠ 0` we cancel it (`mul_eq_zero.mp ... |>.resolve_left hg`) to obtain `a'·u + b'·v = 0`. From there the coprime argument runs verbatim — `b' ∣ a'·u`, then `b' ∣ u` via `IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left`, then cancel `b' ≠ 0` — yielding the PRIMITIVE lattice point `(k·b', −k·a')`. Number theory enters in exactly one step; everything else is `linear_combination`.
mathContext: For $a=ga',\,b=gb'$ with $\gcd(a',b')=1$ and $g\neq 0$, the solutions of $au+bv=0$ are exactly $\{(kb',-ka'):k\in\mathbb{Z}\}=\mathbb{Z}\cdot(b',-a')$, the kernel of $(u,v)\mapsto au+bv$. The generator is the PRIMITIVE vector $(b',-a')=(b/g,-a/g)$.

title: Uniqueness by Differencing; the Converse Is a Ring Identity
content: `general_unique` differences two solutions of `a·x + b·y = c` to get `a·(x₂−x₁) + b·(y₂−y₁) = 0`, then applies `general_homogeneous`: the two solutions differ by one PRIMITIVE step `(k·b', −k·a')`. The converse `general_param` is the one-line `ring` identity `a·(x + k·b') + b·(y − k·a') = a·x + b·y` (after substituting the decomposition). Together they say the solution set is a full coset of `ℤ·(b', −a')`.
mathContext: The solution set of $ax+by=c$ (when non-empty) is the coset $\{(x_0+kb',\,y_0-ka'):k\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ of the primitive homogeneous lattice. Differencing reduces uniqueness to the homogeneous case.

title: Bézout Solvability: a·x + b·y = c iff g ∣ c
content: `general_solvable_iff` is the solvability half, independent of the coset structure. Forward: `a·x + b·y = g·(a'·x + b'·y)` is visibly a multiple of `g`. Backward: coprimality `IsCoprime a' b'` unpacks to `u·a' + v·b' = 1`, so for `c = g·c'` the explicit pair `(c'·u, c'·v)` solves the equation — verified by `linear_combination g·c'·huv`. This is exactly why `6·x + 9·y = 7` has no solution: `3 ∤ 7`.
mathContext: $ax+by=c$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$ iff $\gcd(a,b)\mid c$. The 'if' direction is constructive: scale a Bézout witness for the coprime cofactors by $c/g$.
prerequisites: IsCoprime unfolding to a Bézout identity

title: From Abstract Decomposition to the Actual Integer gcd
content: `int_admits_decomp` discharges the decomposition hypotheses for any `a, b : ℤ` with `b ≠ 0`. First `gcd a b > 0`: if it were `0`, then `(gcd a b : ℤ) ∣ b` (`Int.gcd_dvd_right`) would force `b = 0` (`zero_dvd_iff`). Then `Int.exists_gcd_one'` supplies `g = gcd`, primitive cofactors `a', b'` with `Int.gcd a' b' = 1`, and `a = a'·g`, `b = b'·g`; `Int.isCoprime_iff_gcd_eq_one` upgrades the gcd equation to `IsCoprime a' b'`, and `b' ≠ 0` follows since `b = b'·g ≠ 0`. `int_general_unique` then packages the classification taking only `a, b : ℤ` and `b ≠ 0`.
mathContext: Every $a,b$ not both zero factor as $a=a'g,\,b=b'g$ with $g=\gcd(a,b)>0$ and $\gcd(a',b')=1$; the cofactors $a'=a/g,\,b'=b/g$ generate the primitive lattice $\mathbb{Z}\cdot(b',-a')$.

title: (6, 9): The Primitive Step Is (3, −2), Not (9, −6)
content: For the NON-coprime pair `(6,9)`, `g = 3` and the primitive cofactors are `(a',b') = (2,3)`. The solutions `(2,0)` and `(−1,2)` of `6·x + 9·y = 12` differ by the single primitive step `k = −1` along `(b', −a') = (3, −2)` — `ex69_family` exhibits the whole family `6·(2 + k·3) + 9·(0 − k·2) = 12`. This is the crux of dropping coprimality: the naïve lattice `ℤ·(b, −a) = ℤ·(9, −6)` would skip two of every three solutions; the correct generator is the primitive `(3, −2)`. `ex69_unsolvable` shows `6·x + 9·y = 7` has no solution because `3 ∤ 7`.
mathContext: All integer solutions of $6x+9y=12$ are $(2+3k,\,-2k)$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ — step $(3,-2)$, period one third of $(9,-6)$. And $6x+9y=7$ is unsolvable since $\gcd(6,9)=3\nmid 7$.
